opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this came out of our work at METR on measuring the length of tasks AI agents can complete, the "time horizon" work. When we plotted model performance against how long tasks take humans, we saw a pretty clean trend. But a natural objection is that our tasks are kind of clean: well-specified, automatically scorable, self-contained. Real work isn't like that. So we wanted to know whether models do worse on tasks that look more like real-world work, and whether that changes the story.

To get at that, we came up with a set of what we called "messiness factors." These are properties like: Is the task resource-limited? Does it have a clear feedback signal, or do you have to figure out whether you're on track? Is the environment novel or static? Does it involve interacting with other agents or real-time dynamics? Is it underspecified, so you have to infer what's actually wanted? Can you recover from mistakes, or are some actions irreversible? We rated each task on these and summed them into a rough messiness score.

There were two main findings. First, yes, models do noticeably worse on messier tasks, even controlling for how long the task takes a human. That fits the intuition that a lot of what makes real work hard for current agents isn't raw length or difficulty. It's dealing with ambiguity, missing feedback, and figuring out what's being asked. Second, and to me this was more interesting, the rate of improvement over time looked roughly similar for messier and less messy tasks. So messy tasks weren't plateauing while clean ones kept improving. Models were behind on messy tasks, but they seemed to be getting better at a similar pace.

I'd add some big caveats. Even our "messiest" tasks are much less messy than a lot of real jobs. They're still tasks we could build and score in a benchmark, which selects against the hardest kinds of messiness. And the messiness ratings were somewhat subjective, with a fairly small number of tasks. So I don't think you can conclude "messiness doesn't matter for forecasting." What you can say is that within the range we could measure, we didn't see evidence that messiness is a wall.

As a way to explain successes and failures, I find it useful because it points at a gap between benchmark performance and real-world usefulness. People notice that models crush impressive benchmarks but then struggle with what seems like a simple job at work. Often the difference is that the work task is messy: unclear success criteria, lots of implicit context, no tests telling you you're done. So messiness is a decent first-pass vocabulary for why the impressive demos and the disappointing deployments can both be true at once.

r001.rationale: It reports a clear trend between human task duration and model performance, and says the analysis controlled for how long a task takes humans.

r002.rationale: It says messiness ratings were subjective, but does not identify disagreement over what counts as a messy task.

r003.rationale: It mentions inferring what is wanted in underspecified tasks, but does not clearly distinguish deciding what to do from carrying out an already specified objective.

r004.rationale: It discusses a gap between benchmark performance and disappointing deployments, but does not identify the lack of developer speedup in David Rein’s team’s randomized controlled trial as a research question.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this came out of work we did at METR trying to understand the gap between how AI systems do on benchmarks and how they do on real-world tasks. The puzzle is pretty stark: models are crushing competitive programming problems and PhD-level science questions, but when you actually try to get them to do a day of a software engineer's job, they often fall over in ways that are kind of embarrassing.

The hypothesis we were exploring is that benchmark tasks tend to be clean in a bunch of ways that real tasks aren't. So we tried to make that concrete. We came up with a list of properties, around sixteen or so, that make a task "messy." Things like: is the task novel or is it a well-trodden pattern? Is the problem fully specified, or do you have to figure out what's actually being asked? Does it require real-time coordination with other people or systems? Is the feedback loop tight, or do you only find out whether you succeeded much later? Is there a lot of implicit context that a human would have from being embedded in the environment? Is it resource-constrained? Are there irrecoverable mistakes? And then we scored tasks on how many of these properties they had.

What we found is that on low-messiness tasks, the time horizon of what models can do, meaning the length of task measured by how long it takes humans, is growing very fast, doubling something like every seven months or faster. On the messier tasks, performance is noticeably worse at any given point in time. But the interesting thing is that the rate of improvement doesn't look obviously slower on messy tasks. So it's less like messiness is a wall and more like it's an offset. Models are maybe a year or two behind on messy stuff relative to clean stuff, but they're catching up on both.

I'd say I hold that pretty loosely though. Our messy tasks were still tasks we could put in an evaluation, which means they were still a lot cleaner than actual work. The really messy end of the distribution, where there's no clear success criterion and you have to talk to five people to figure out what the task even is, we mostly can't measure yet. So the extrapolation to "messy work will be automated in two years" is doing a lot of work that the data doesn't fully support. But as a frame for why the same model can look superhuman and incompetent in the same afternoon, I think it's a pretty useful one.

r001.rationale: It defines task length by how long humans take and reports performance differences by messiness, but does not say human completion time explains variation in model success across tasks.

r002.rationale: It notes limits in measuring very messy work, but does not identify disagreement about what counts as a messy task.

r003.rationale: It mentions tasks that require figuring out what is being asked, but does not distinguish deciding what to do from carrying out an already specified objective.

r004.rationale: It describes the benchmark-to-real-world performance gap as a research motivation, but does not mention the randomized controlled trial or its finding of no developer speedup.

astra-6.text:
I think task messiness is a useful lens, but I’m skeptical that it’s a complete explanation. There are several things that can make a task messy: the goal might be underspecified, the information you need might be scattered across different places, or you might need to take a lot of actions and recover when something goes wrong. Those seem like potentially different limitations, even if they all produce the impression that a system struggles with messy tasks.

There’s also a risk of circularity. If we call the tasks AI succeeds at clean and the tasks it fails at messy, we haven’t really explained anything. What I’d like is to specify those properties in advance and then see whether they predict performance. Can you take roughly the same underlying problem, make the instructions less explicit or introduce irrelevant information, and reliably make the system worse?

So I’d treat messiness as a starting point for investigating failures. It points toward things that benchmarks can leave out, but you still want to identify which particular feature is causing the difficulty.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention the time humans need to complete a task or connect it to variation in AI success.

r002.rationale: It lists several possible features of messy tasks and warns about circular definitions, but does not identify disagreement over what counts as messy as a challenge.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish deciding what to do in real-world work from carrying out a task with a specified objective.

r004.rationale: It does not mention benchmark performance, the team's randomized controlled trial, or the research question of explaining the gap between them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think task messiness is a useful lens, though I’d be careful about treating it as a single property that explains everything. There’s a difference between how hard the central intellectual problem is and how much surrounding stuff you have to get right to actually complete the task.

For example, a math problem can be very difficult but relatively clean: you’re given a precise statement, and there’s a clear notion of a correct answer. Something like fixing a bug in a large codebase might involve easier individual reasoning steps, but you have to find the relevant files, understand undocumented assumptions, get the environment working, and check that your change didn’t break something else. There are many more opportunities to get derailed.

That can help explain why a system looks extremely impressive on a benchmark but is frustrating to use for a seemingly mundane task. The benchmark may isolate precisely the part it’s good at, while the real task requires a whole chain of things to work reliably.

But I wouldn’t conclude that messiness is some permanent barrier. You can make tasks cleaner through better tools and interfaces, and systems can get better at handling the surrounding complications. The question is how much of the gap comes from those complications, versus a limitation in the underlying reasoning. Just calling a task messy doesn’t settle that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task complexity and surrounding complications, but does not say that the time humans need to complete a task explains variation in AI success.

r002.rationale: It cautions that messiness is not a single property, but does not identify disagreement about what counts as messy as a challenge.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts clean benchmarks with messy real tasks, but does not distinguish choosing what to do in real-world work from carrying out a task with an already specified objective.

r004.rationale: It mentions a gap between impressive benchmark results and frustrating real-world use, but does not identify the gap with the lack of developer speedup in Rein's team's randomized controlled trial.
